words.intro: For forty years a fence ran through the middle of Germany. At Point Alpha in the Rhön you can still walk the old border path, past the watchtowers, with the people who remember it.

grammar[0].fact: Point Alpha, on the border between Hesse and Thuringia, was a US Army observation post in the Fulda Gap: the place where NATO expected the Soviet tanks to come. The Americans left in 1989, and the post is now a museum.

document.intro: A real sign at the US post, in English and German. It’s the same text twice, so use it to read the German. It’s from an old machine: ae for ä, ue for ü.
document.fact: German can always be written without dots: *ae, oe, ue, ss*. Old typewriters and signs did this, and it’s what you still type into an airline form. So Herr Müller appears as MUELLER in his passport’s machine-readable line.

reading.intro: Lena’s grandmother, Oma Erna, grew up in a village in Thuringia, 400 metres from the fence. Her sister Gerda was in the village on the other side. Lena has brought Maya along to Point Alpha, the old border, and Oma Erna tells the story as she walks.
reading.photos[0].caption: Ein Schild am Grenzmuseum: Teilstück der ehemaligen Sperranlage.
reading.fact: The inner German border ran for 1,393 km. Today the former death strip is a nature reserve, the *Grünes Band*, one long green line of rare birds and orchids from the Baltic to Bavaria. It exists because for forty years, nobody could go in.
